title: SHE COVERED HER FACE THE MOMENT SHE SAW HIM… BUT WHAT HAPPENED NEXT REVEALS SOMETHING BEAUTIFUL ABOUT GOD’S TIMING
paragraphs: SHE COVERED HER FACE THE MOMENT SHE SAW HIM… BUT WHAT HAPPENED NEXT REVEALS SOMETHING BEAUTIFUL ABOUT GOD’S TIMING

Before Rebekah ever heard Isaac say, “I love you,” she had already left everything familiar behind. And the moment she lifted her eyes toward the man she would marry, she reached for her veil. But behind that quiet gesture is a story about faith, surrender, grief, and the God who is still writing beautiful chapters when we cannot see what comes next.

“And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel. For she had said unto the servant, What man is this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant had said, It is my master: therefore she took a vail, and covered herself.” — Genesis 24:64–65 (KJV)
She saw a man walking across a field.
She did not know the sound of his laughter.
She did not know how he spoke when he was tired, how he handled disappointment, or what his face looked like when grief returned in the middle of the night.
She had never sat across from him at a meal.
They had never shared a conversation.
And yet, this was the man she had traveled so far to meet.
Rebekah reached for her veil.
One small movement.
One quiet moment in the wilderness.
And nearly four thousand years later, that moment still speaks.
But perhaps not in the way you expect.
Because this is not merely a story about a woman covering her face before meeting her future husband.
It is a story about two people carrying different kinds of uncertainty toward a future neither could fully see.
One was leaving home.
The other was living with loss.
And God, in His providence, was bringing their stories together.
There is something deeply human about that.
Because sometimes the greatest changes in our lives begin while we are still carrying questions we cannot answer.
Sometimes we are asked to leave what is familiar before we know what the future will feel like.
And sometimes, while we are grieving what we have lost, God is already preparing something we cannot yet recognize.
Not every journey ends in marriage.
Not every prayer receives the answer we imagined.
But Genesis 24 invites us to consider something far greater than a romantic encounter.
It invites us to trust the God whose faithfulness is not limited by our ability to see tomorrow.
And to understand why Rebekah covered her face, we must first understand what she had already surrendered.
Abraham was growing old.
His wife Sarah had died.
His son Isaac remained unmarried.
And Abraham was deeply concerned about the continuation of the covenant promises God had given him.
This was no ordinary family arrangement.
God had promised Abraham that through his offspring, blessing would reach the nations (Genesis 12:1–3; 22:18).
Isaac was the son through whom that covenant line would continue.
So Abraham sent his trusted servant to his relatives to find a wife for Isaac.
The servant traveled to Mesopotamia, carrying gifts and a serious responsibility.
And when he reached the city of Nahor, he prayed.
He asked the LORD to grant him success and to show covenant kindness to Abraham.
Then he watched.
A young woman came to draw water.
Her name was Rebekah.
The servant asked for a drink.
She gave him water.
Then she offered to draw water for his camels as well.
Read that carefully.
The servant had not asked her to water the camels.
She volunteered.
And watering camels after a long journey was no small gesture.
It required effort.
Time.
Repeated trips to the well.
Rebekah's generosity was not merely something she said.
It was something she did.
Long before she knew the full significance of this encounter, her character was visible in the ordinary work of her day.
That should make us think.
We often want God to reveal our great purpose while overlooking the opportunities to practice faithfulness directly in front of us.
We want to know who we will become.
Who we will marry.
Where we will go.
When the breakthrough will happen.
But character is often formed in the unnoticed moments.
In how we treat people who cannot repay us.
In what we do when nobody is applauding.
In whether our kindness survives inconvenience.
Rebekah did not know that offering water would become part of a story preserved in Scripture.
She was simply responding generously to someone in need.
And there is a quiet lesson here.
You do not have to know the significance of every moment to be faithful in it.
The servant recognized the remarkable answer to his prayer.
He worshiped the LORD.
He explained his mission to Rebekah's family.
And eventually, the question became personal.
Would Rebekah go?
Her family called her and asked directly.
The Hebrew of Genesis 24:58 records the question:
הֲתֵלְכִי עִם־הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה
Ha-tel'khi im-ha'ish hazzeh?
“Will you go with this man?”
Her answer was astonishingly brief.
אֵלֵךְ
Elekh.
“I will go.”
Two English words.
One Hebrew word.
A decision that would change her life.
She was leaving her family, her homeland, and everything familiar to travel toward a man she had never met.
We should not pretend that Scripture tells us every emotion she experienced.
It does not say whether she trembled, cried, or struggled to sleep that night.
But the magnitude of her decision is unmistakable.
She agreed to go.
And this is where the story begins to reach beyond ancient history.
Because perhaps you know something about leaving.
Not necessarily leaving a country.
Perhaps you left a relationship that was destroying you.
Perhaps you walked away from a life of sin that once felt comfortable.
Perhaps obedience to Christ has cost you friendships, approval, opportunities, or the illusion of control.
Perhaps you are standing at the edge of a decision, knowing what Scripture calls you to do but still afraid of what obedience may cost.
Rebekah's words were simple.
“I will go.”
But simple words can carry enormous consequences.
And for followers of Jesus, surrender is not merely saying that we trust God.
It is learning to obey Him when obedience becomes costly.
Still, we must be careful.

Rebekah's particular journey was part of God's covenant purposes for Abraham's family. It is not a universal command to accept uncertain relationships, ignore warning signs, or make major decisions without wisdom.
Biblical faith is not recklessness.
And trusting God does not mean abandoning discernment.
But her willingness to leave reminds us that faith often involves moving forward without possessing every answer.
Now picture the journey.
Days of travel.
Miles of unfamiliar landscape.
The slow rhythm of the caravan.
The growing distance between Rebekah and the home she had always known.
Somewhere ahead was Isaac.
But what was Isaac doing?
This is where the story becomes unexpectedly tender.
Genesis 24:63 says Isaac went out into the field toward evening.
The Hebrew verb used there is:
לָשׂוּחַ
Lasuach.
It is an uncommon verb whose precise nuance is debated. The KJV translates the phrase as Isaac going out “to meditate,” while other translations understand it as walking or reflecting in the field.
We should not build an entire doctrine around a word whose meaning is uncertain.
But the scene itself is clear.
Isaac was outside in the field at evening when he looked up and saw camels approaching.
And there is something important about the man waiting there.
Isaac was not entering this moment untouched by sorrow.
His mother Sarah had died.
Genesis 23 records her death.
And Genesis 24:67 later tells us that Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.
That detail changes the emotional weight of the entire encounter.
Rebekah was arriving at the beginning of a new chapter.
Isaac was still carrying the grief of an earlier one.
One was stepping into the unknown.
The other was learning how to live after loss.
And their lives were about to meet.
Maybe that is why this passage feels so personal.
Because life rarely waits until we are completely healed before presenting us with new responsibilities.
Sometimes we are still grieving when tomorrow arrives.
Still recovering when someone needs us.
Still learning how to trust when another door opens.
And there are wounds that do not disappear simply because life moves forward.
If you have buried someone you loved, you understand.
There are ordinary moments when the absence becomes almost unbearable.
An empty chair.
A familiar voice you will never hear again.
A name you still want to call.
A memory that arrives without warning.
And the world keeps moving.
Isaac knew something of that kind of loss.
Scripture does not describe every tear he shed.
But it tells us enough to know that his mother's death still mattered.
Then, across the field, the caravan approached.
Rebekah lifted her eyes.
She saw Isaac.
And she asked the servant who he was.
When the servant identified him, she took her veil and covered herself.
Here is the Hebrew wording from Genesis 24:65:
וַתִּקַּח הַצָּעִיף וַתִּתְכָּס
Vattiqqach hatza'if vattitkas.
“And she took the veil and covered herself.”
The Hebrew noun צָעִיף (tsa'if) refers to a veil or covering.
The text describes an actual action, not merely a poetic symbol.
Rebekah covered herself upon learning that the man approaching was Isaac.
In the ancient cultural setting, this gesture is commonly understood in connection with modesty, decorum, and the formal meeting of a prospective bride and bridegroom.
But Scripture does not explicitly tell us her inner motive.
It does not say she covered her face because she was ashamed.
It does not say she was afraid of Isaac.
It does not say she was hiding secret sins.
And it certainly does not establish a command that every Christian woman must wear a veil when meeting her future husband.
Those conclusions would go beyond what Genesis actually says.
The beauty of the passage does not require us to invent details.
The truth is already powerful enough.
A woman who had chosen to leave home was now standing at the threshold of the future she had agreed to enter.
And she covered herself.
That was the moment.
But it was not the end of the story.
The servant told Isaac everything that had happened.
Everything.
The journey.
The prayer.
The encounter at the well.
The generosity of Rebekah.
The response of her family.
The decision that brought her there.
And then Genesis 24:67 gives us one of the most tender descriptions of marriage in the book of Genesis.
“And Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah's tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her: and Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.” — Genesis 24:67 (KJV)
He loved her.
Let those words settle.
In an account shaped by family arrangements, travel, covenant promises, and an unfamiliar future, Scripture makes a point of telling us that Isaac loved Rebekah.
The Hebrew says:
וַיֶּאֱהָבֶהָ
Vayye'ehaveha.
“And he loved her.”
And Isaac was comforted.
The Hebrew uses the verb וַיִּנָּחֵם (vayyinnachem), expressing that he received comfort or consolation.
Not that Sarah ceased to matter.
Not that his grief had never existed.
Not that Rebekah somehow replaced his mother.
But that comfort entered his life after bereavement.
There is a difference between replacing what was lost and receiving comfort after loss.
The Bible does not ask us to erase the people we have loved.
It does not teach that a new blessing makes an old wound meaningless.
And it does not promise that every grieving person will receive a spouse as the answer to their sorrow.
But it does show us that grief and comfort can exist within the same human story.
That is a truth some of us desperately need.
Because perhaps you have believed that your best days ended when someone walked away.
Perhaps you have convinced yourself that because a relationship failed, your future has failed too.
Perhaps you are ashamed of the choices you made when you were lonely.
Perhaps you keep replaying conversations, wishing you could go back and become someone different.
And perhaps you have been carrying a quiet question into every new morning.
“Lord, is there still anything good ahead of me?”
Listen carefully.
Genesis 24 is not a guarantee that God will give every person the marriage they desire.
It is not a promise that waiting long enough will make someone return.
And it is not permission to treat romance as the ultimate evidence of God's favor.
Some faithful Christians marry.
Some remain single.
Some experience widowhood, separation, or painful disappointment.
Their worth before God is not determined by their relationship status.
The deeper hope of Scripture is not that every person will find an Isaac or a Rebekah.
The deeper hope is that God's covenant faithfulness ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ.
And that is where this story becomes greater than a wedding.
Because the marriage of Isaac and Rebekah belongs to the unfolding history of God's promise to Abraham.
From Abraham came Isaac.
From Isaac came Jacob.
Through the generations of Israel, God's redemptive plan continued.
And in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came into the world.
Matthew 1:1 identifies Him as the son of Abraham.
Galatians 3:16 directs our attention to Christ as the promised offspring in whom God's covenant purposes find their fulfillment.
And Galatians 3:29 declares that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise.
That is the greater story.
Not simply that Rebekah found a husband.
But that God remained faithful to the promise through which salvation would ultimately be proclaimed to the nations.
A marriage in Genesis became part of the family history through which the Savior entered the world.
And the Savior did not come merely to improve our circumstances.
He came to rescue sinners.
He came to bear our guilt.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to do what no human relationship could ever accomplish.
Because there is a loneliness deeper than being unmarried.
There is a separation more serious than being abandoned by another person.
There is the reality of sin.
The guilt we cannot erase by pretending.
The pride we defend.
The bitterness we nurture.
The secret compromises we excuse.
The people we have wounded.
The ways we have rejected the God who made us.
We can hide those things from other people.
We can dress beautifully.
Smile convincingly.
Post inspiring words.
Serve in church.
Sing every worship song.
And still carry a heart that needs repentance.
That is the scandal beneath our carefully managed appearances.
Not merely that people have misunderstood us.
But that we have sinned against a holy God.
And here is the astonishing grace of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come because we were already righteous.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had overcome every temptation.
Not after we had become impressive enough to deserve mercy.
Christ died for sinners.
And He rose again.
The cross exposes the seriousness of our sin.
The resurrection announces the victory of our Savior.
This is why the Gospel is not simply a message about finding happiness.
It is the announcement that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
And it is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not pretending that sin never happened.
It is turning from sin toward God.
It is bringing what we would rather conceal into the light of His truth.
It is refusing to make peace with what nailed our Savior to the cross.
And it is trusting that the mercy of Christ is greater than the guilt we bring to Him.
Maybe you have spent years covering things.
Covering your disappointment.
Covering your shame.
Covering the wounds of betrayal.
Covering the fact that you have slowly drifted away from God.
You know how to answer, “I'm fine.”
You know how to smile when your heart is exhausted.
You know how to encourage everyone else while secretly wondering whether you can survive another difficult season.
But there is something you need to hear.
Rebekah's veil was a real cultural gesture in an ancient marriage narrative. It was not a biblical symbol of hidden sin.
Yet her story can still cause us to examine the things we hide in our own lives.
And when we do, the Gospel gives us an answer far greater than pretending.
We do not need to manufacture an image of perfection before coming to Jesus.
We need to come to Him in repentance and faith.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Think about that.
Not merely tolerated.
Not merely given another chance to impress people.
Forgiven.
Cleansed.
Because of the faithfulness and righteousness of God, grounded in the saving work of Christ.
And when Jesus saves someone, He does not simply attach a religious label to their old life.
He begins the work of transformation.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
That does not mean believers never struggle again.
It does not mean every consequence of past sin disappears.
It does not mean healing always happens quickly.
But it means our past no longer has the final authority to define who we are in Christ.
And perhaps that is the sentence you have needed for years.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
That is what we mean when we say:
Not that scandal is beautiful.
Not that sin is harmless.
Not that every painful situation will turn into the outcome we wanted.
But that Jesus Christ can redeem people who have sinned, restore those who have wandered, and transform lives that once seemed hopeless.
He does not rewrite history by pretending evil was good.
He rewrites our future through forgiveness, redemption, and the new life that comes through Him.
And that brings us back to the field.
Back to the approaching camels.
Back to Rebekah's veil.
Back to Isaac, who had known grief.
Two lives meeting within a much larger story.
Neither could see everything that lay ahead.
Their marriage would not be free from difficulty.
Later chapters of Genesis reveal family tensions, favoritism, and painful consequences within their household.
The Bible does not present Isaac and Rebekah as flawless people living in a perfect marriage.
That matters.
Because the faithfulness of God does not depend upon His people becoming flawless characters in a romantic story.
It rests upon His own character and promises.
And in the end, the most important Bridegroom in Scripture is not Isaac.
It is Jesus.
The New Testament describes Christ's relationship with His church through the imagery of marriage.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
Revelation 19:7 speaks of the marriage of the Lamb.
These passages are not claiming that every detail of Genesis 24 secretly represents a separate aspect of salvation.
We should not force allegories into Scripture that the text does not establish.
But we can recognize the beautiful direction of the biblical story.
From the covenant family of Abraham to the coming of Christ.
From the promises of God to their fulfillment in the Savior.
From human marriages, with all their limitations, to the perfect covenant love of Jesus for His people.
Isaac loved Rebekah.
Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
And unlike any earthly bridegroom, Jesus is the sinless Savior whose love is demonstrated through His sacrificial death and victorious resurrection.
That is where our hope must finally rest.
Not in being chosen by another human being.
But in belonging to Christ through faith.
Not in having every dream fulfilled on earth.
But in knowing the One who promises eternal life.
Not in a future without hardship.
But in the faithfulness of the Lord who will never abandon His people.
So if you are reading this while waiting for something, do not turn Genesis 24 into a prediction about when your breakthrough will arrive.
Instead, allow it to remind you of the God who keeps His promises.
If you are grieving, you do not have to pretend you are healed.
If you are single, you are not spiritually incomplete.
If you are married, remember that love must be practiced through faithfulness, humility, and sacrifice.
If you have fallen into sin, do not use grace as permission to remain there.
Repent.
Come back to Christ.
If you are exhausted from trying to appear strong, remember that your Savior already knows the truth about you.
You can stop performing.
You can pray.
You can confess.
You can seek help.
You can begin walking in obedience again.
And if you have never trusted Jesus Christ as your Savior, do not settle for admiring the beauty of a Bible story while missing the Lord to whom the Scriptures ultimately point.
Come to Him.
Turn from sin.
Believe the Gospel.
The One who died and rose again is worthy of your trust.
Perhaps your prayer tonight is not eloquent.
Perhaps all you can say is:

“Lord Jesus, I have been hiding. I have been afraid. I have tried to control things that belong in Your hands. Forgive my sins. Teach me to trust You. Heal what is broken according to Your wisdom. Change what needs to change in me. And whether my circumstances change quickly or slowly, help me remain faithful to You.”
That is not a magical formula.
But it may express the honest surrender your heart has been resisting.
And sometimes honesty before God is where a long season of pretending finally ends.
If this message has reached something deep within you, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not have to disclose private details publicly. A few sincere words are enough.
Your story may remind another person that they are not alone in the struggle.
There may be someone reading quietly who has not prayed in months.
Someone who feels ashamed to return to church.
Someone who believes their mistakes have placed them beyond forgiveness.
Your words might encourage that person to open the Bible again, seek a faithful Christian community, and turn toward Christ.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page.
But because the Gospel deserves to be heard beyond the people who already know it.
Send it privately to someone who is searching for hope.
Invite someone who is skeptical about Christianity to read the actual Scriptures and consider the person of Jesus.
Our desire is to continue sharing biblical truth, Gospel-centered encouragement, repentance, discipleship, and the hope of redemption through Jesus Christ.
And for those who want to walk more deeply with this ministry, there is another invitation.
If you have been looking for a practical way to support Christian teaching and outreach, this is one opportunity to do so.
But I want to be clear about something important.
Biblical giving is not a transaction through which we buy blessings.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And you never need to pay to receive the grace of Jesus Christ.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The purpose is to help keep the ministry sustainable while offering resources and reminders that can encourage everyday Christian living.
We want struggling believers to be strengthened.
We want those who have wandered to hear the call to repentance.
We want families to discover resources that encourage prayer, Scripture reading, and Christ-centered living.
We want the name of Jesus to be exalted.
If you believe in that mission, if you have benefited from these messages, and if you are financially able to help sustain this work, I warmly invite you to become a monthly supporter.
You can still be part of this mission.
Read the Scriptures.
Pray for the ministry.
Use the free library.
Grow in your local church.
And most importantly, keep following Jesus.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build a crowd around Gospel Warrior.
It is to point people to the Savior.
One day, our posts will be forgotten.
Our platforms may disappear.
But the Word of the Lord endures forever.
And the people who belong to Christ have a hope that reaches beyond every temporary success, every painful disappointment, and even death itself.
Now think about Rebekah one last time.
She lifted her eyes.
She saw Isaac.
She covered herself with a veil.
And she stepped into a future she had never experienced before.
She could not have known every joy or difficulty that marriage would bring.
She could not have seen every generation that would follow.
She could not have imagined the full unfolding of God's redemptive purpose through the family into which she was entering.
But the God who had made His promise to Abraham remained faithful.
And generations later, Jesus Christ came.
The promised Savior.
The crucified Redeemer.
The risen Lord.
The One in whom sinners find forgiveness and believers receive eternal hope.
So perhaps the question you should carry away from this story is not, “When will God send my Isaac?”
Perhaps the greater question is:
“Am I willing to trust and obey Jesus, even when I cannot see the entire road ahead?”
Because the greatest love story in Scripture is not about a woman finding a husband in a field.
It is about a holy Savior giving His life to redeem sinners and bring them back to God.
And when that truth finally reaches your heart, you begin to understand why grace is more beautiful than any ending you could have written for yourself.
The veil was only a moment in Rebekah's story. But the mercy of Jesus can change the whole direction of yours.
